section.title: Jonah's Anger and God's Mercy
section.sectionRationale: The book's final movement turns from the city to the prophet's heart: Jonah's anger at God's mercy, the object lesson of the plant, the worm, and the wind, and God's closing question that the book leaves hanging. It is one unit exposing the resentment of grace.
section.thesis: The prophet is furious that God is merciful, and God answers his anger not with wrath but with a plant, a worm, and a question that presses the reader to share His compassion for a lost world.
section.frameNote: Three scenes: Jonah's angry prayer and God's question; the plant, the worm, and the wind; God's closing appeal that ends the book unresolved.

verses.text: Jonah, however, was greatly {{raah|displeased}}, and he became angry.

So he prayed to the LORD, saying, “O LORD, is this not what I said while I was still in my own country? This is why I was so quick to flee toward Tarshish. I knew that You are a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger, abounding in {{chesed|loving devotion}}, One who {{nacham|relents}} from sending disaster.
And now, O LORD, please take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live.”
But the LORD replied, “Have you any right to be angry?”

units.label: The plant, the worm, and the wind

verses.text: Then Jonah left the city and sat down east of it, where he made himself a shelter and sat in its shade to see what would happen to the city.
So the LORD God {{manah|appointed}} a vine, and it grew up to provide shade over Jonah’s head to ease his discomfort, and Jonah was greatly pleased with the plant.
When dawn came the next day, God {{manah|appointed}} a worm that attacked the plant so that it withered.
As the sun was rising, God {{manah|appointed}} a scorching east wind, and the sun beat down on Jonah’s head so that he grew faint and wished to die, saying, “It is better for me to die than to live.”

units.label: God's closing question
units.note: should I not care for Nineveh?

verses.text: Then God asked Jonah, “Have you any right to be angry about the plant?” “I do,” he replied. “I am angry enough to die!”
But the LORD said, “You {{chus|cared}} about the plant, which you neither tended nor made grow. It sprang up in a night and perished in a night.
So should I not {{chus|care}} about the {{gadol|great}} city of Nineveh, which has more than 120,000 people who cannot tell their right hand from their left, and many cattle as well?”

raah.gloss: Evil, calamity, or displeasure. The very word for Nineveh's wickedness and the threatened disaster is now used of Jonah's reaction: God's mercy was, literally, a great evil to Jonah. The book turns the word back on the prophet, exposing his twisted heart.

chesed.gloss: Loving devotion, steadfast love, covenant faithfulness. Jonah quotes God's own self-description from Exodus 34:6; he knows God abounds in this love, and that is exactly why he ran, unwilling to see it poured out on his enemies.

nacham.gloss: To relent, be moved to compassion, or change a course of action. Jonah names God as One who relents from sending disaster. What draws worship from others draws only resentment from Jonah, who cannot bear that God relents toward Nineveh.

manah.gloss: To appoint, assign, or ordain. As He appointed the fish, God now appoints a plant, a worm, and a wind, three small agents to teach one stubborn man. The word shows God patiently marshalling creation to reach Jonah's heart.

chus.gloss: To pity, spare, or have compassion on. God's closing argument turns on it: Jonah pitied a plant he did not make; should not God pity a city of people He made? It is the compassion the whole book has been driving toward.

gadol.gloss: Great, large. The great city that opened the book returns at its close. Nineveh's greatness is now measured not by its threat but by the multitude of souls in it, more than 120,000, whom God will not lightly destroy.

basic.context: Nineveh is spared, and Jonah is furious. He admits this is why he ran: he knew God was merciful and did not want his enemies forgiven. He even asks to die. So God gives him a plant for shade, then a worm to kill it, then a scorching wind, and asks a pointed question: if Jonah cares this much about a plant, should not God care about a whole city of people?
basic.hermeneutics: The book ends not with a tidy resolution but with a question left hanging for the reader. Jonah's anger at grace is meant to expose our own hearts. When God asks whether He should care about Nineveh, the answer is obvious, and we are left to ask whether we truly share His heart for people we would rather see judged.
basic.originalLanguages: The word for evil, ra'ah, once used of Nineveh's wickedness, is now used of Jonah's mood: God's mercy was a great evil to him. Jonah quotes God's own words about His loving devotion, chesed, and His relenting, nacham. God appoints, manah, a plant, worm, and wind, and the climax turns on chus, to pity or spare.
basic.typology: Jonah, angry outside the city that his enemies were spared, is the dark mirror of Christ, who wept over the city and prayed forgiveness for His enemies as He was killed. The contrast throws the mercy of Jesus into sharp relief.
basic.christ: Jonah resented mercy to his enemies and wanted them dead; Jesus loved His enemies and died for them, praying, Father, forgive them. Where Jonah would not go and would not care, Christ came, cared, and gave His life. He is the true and better Jonah with a heart full of compassion.
basic.god: We learn that God is gracious, compassionate, slow to anger, and abounding in love, that He pursues even His hardened prophet with patience rather than wrath, and that He genuinely cares for people who do not yet know Him, a whole city who cannot tell right from left.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 34 is the self-description of God that Jonah quotes. Luke 15 shows the elder brother who resents mercy to the returning sinner, just like Jonah. And Luke 19 shows Jesus weeping over a city rather than gloating over its ruin.
basic.oneStory: The book ends by pressing God's heart for the nations onto every reader. God's last word is a question about compassion for a lost city, and it looks straight ahead to Christ, who does not merely pity the nations but gives Himself to save them, and to a church sent to love the very people it once feared.

context.literary:
Jonah 4 balances Jonah 1 and 2 as closely as chapter 3 balanced the opening. The prophet who would rather die than obey in chapter 1, and who prays from the fish in chapter 2, now prays from beneath a shelter in chapter 4, and the content of the prayers is the most revealing thing in the book. In chapter 2 he quotes the Psalms and ends with a vow to sacrifice with thanksgiving. In chapter 4 he quotes God's own self-description, but as a charge sheet. The same man who was saved from the deep is grieved to see another city saved from the edge.

The chapter is built on questions. God asks 'Have you any right to be angry?' in verse 4, asks it again about the plant in verse 9, and closes the book with a question in verse 11 that goes unanswered. Jonah's own speeches grow shorter and angrier: a prayer in verses 2 and 3, a wish to die in verse 8, and a retort in verse 9, 'I am angry enough to die!' The Lord's replies grow longer and more patient. By the end the argument is entirely one-sided on the page, yet the book simply stops, leaving the reader to supply the answer that Jonah withholds.

The narrator also strings together four acts of God that he calls appointments: the vine, the worm, the wind, and in the first half the great fish. The chapter's three-step lesson is staged over a night and a morning: the vine grows, the worm strikes at dawn, the wind rises with the sun. Joy, loss and suffering come in turn, each one appointed by God for the same man, so that the reader sees how a heart is exposed. The deliberate pairing of 'greatly displeased' in verse 1 with 'greatly pleased' in verse 6 shows Jonah's emotions rising and falling with his comfort, not with the fate of a city.

The pattern 'it is better for me to die than to live' recurs in verses 3 and 8 and is quoted back by Jonah in verse 9. The refrain frames the middle of the chapter, and the plant episode is the lens through which the refrain is explained.
context.historical:
Jonah is waiting outside Nineveh, east of the city, in a shelter he made himself, 'to see what would happen,' verse 5. He is still treating the forty days as a question mark. If the Lord has relented, why not wait and watch in case the city reverts? His position says something about the political reality of the age. An Israelite prophet in the eighth century had learned to see Assyria as an enemy to be feared. That Nineveh would later conquer Samaria and carry Israel into exile, 2 Kings 17:6, was a threat any observer might have read into the situation. Jonah's anger is not simply petty; he understands exactly what the survival of Nineveh might cost his own people.

The details of the lesson fit the world of the Near East. The shelter is a sukkah, a booth of branches, the kind of rough shade a traveller or a harvest worker might throw together. The 'scorching east wind' of verse 8 is the hot dry wind that blows in from the desert, which can wither crops and crush the strength of anyone exposed to it. The plant, in Hebrew qiqayon, is named in the BSB footnote as 'possibly the castor oil plant,' a fast-growing plant with large leaves. That it can grow in a night and die in a night suits its character, but ancient translators disagreed about what the word meant, and the identification is a guess.

The population figure of 'more than 120,000 people' is given in the Hebrew as twelve times ten thousand. Great cities in the ancient world were crowded and Nineveh was among the largest, and the writer chooses the figure to answer the weight of one plant. The phrase 'who cannot tell their right hand from their left' means people without moral discernment, not people without a mind. Deuteronomy 1:39 speaks of children who 'did not know good from evil,' and Isaiah 7:15-16 uses the same image for a child too young to choose between good and evil. Whether the phrase refers only to children or to a people ignorant of the true God is debated, and either way it describes those who do not yet know what the Lord requires.

Nineveh, in the end, fell. It was destroyed in 612 BC by a coalition of Babylonians and Medes, a fact consistent with Nahum 3:1 and Zephaniah 2:13. The book of Jonah is not about whether the city lasted, but about how God treats a city while it stands.
context.canonical:
The speech Jonah quotes in verse 2 is the most repeated confession of faith in the Old Testament. It comes from the Lord's own proclamation of His name to Moses after the golden calf, Exodus 34:6-7, and echoes through Numbers 14:18, Psalm 86:15, Psalm 103:8, Psalm 145:8, and Joel 2:13. In nearly every case it is used as a confession of hope: because God is like this, His people may come back. Jonah is the only speaker who turns the confession into a complaint. He also stops short. Exodus 34:7 goes on to say that God 'will by no means leave the guilty unpunished,' but Jonah, like Joel, closes the confession on God's readiness to relent, 'One who relents from sending disaster.' Jonah has lingered on exactly the half that stings him.

Jonah's prayer to die belongs to a series of such prayers in Scripture. Moses asks to be killed when the burden of the people overwhelms him, Numbers 11:15. Elijah, after his victory on Carmel and flight from Jezebel, sits under a broom tree and asks to die, 1 Kings 19:4. In each case God deals with the servant gently. Jonah's case is darker, because the cause is not exhaustion but anger at mercy. The question God asks Jonah is the question He asked Cain, 'Why are you angry?' Genesis 4:6, which places Jonah beside the first angry man in the Bible.

The book ends with a question on the lips of Jesus' parables as well. The father of the prodigal comes out and pleads with the resentful elder brother, Luke 15:28-32, and the parable stops without telling us whether he came in. The master of the vineyard asks, 'Are you envious because I am generous?' Matthew 20:15. Paul gives the theology behind the question: 'I will have mercy on whom I have mercy,' Romans 9:15, and 'God has consigned everyone to disobedience so that He may have mercy on everyone,' Romans 11:32. In Jewish practice the book of Jonah is read on the afternoon of the Day of Atonement, which keeps its message about mercy before the congregation at the point of greatest need.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author ends his book with the prophet, not the city. By chapter 3 the question of Nineveh has been answered: it turned and was spared. The only open question is what the chosen people will do with that mercy. Chapter 4 turns the lens on the reader's own side of the ledger and shows it for what it is. Jonah is a prophet who has been rescued from the deep, who knows God's character better than any reader, and who still would rather see a city destroyed than see God's mercy exercised. The author means the first hearers to see themselves in him.

The author puts the confession of God's character in the mouth of the one person who hates it, and lets the reader notice the irony. 'I knew that You are a gracious and compassionate God' is not an insight Jonah has gained but a reason he fled. The text is making a theological point about orthodoxy: it is possible to say true things about God and resent what they mean. The remedy is not more information. Jonah has the information. What he lacks is the heart of the God he describes.

The author then uses the plant to expose the proportions of Jonah's concern. A man who pities a vine he did not plant or water but enjoyed for a day should be able to understand a God who pities a city He made and sustains. The closing question, 'should I not care about the great city of Nineveh,' is a rhetorical question, but the author withholds the reply deliberately. The first hearers were meant to finish the book by answering aloud, and to find that they cannot answer honestly without changing.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records Jonah's anger, his death wish and his defence of his own indignation. It is not endorsing any of them. God's response to the prophet is not agreement but patient correction, and the story's silence at the end is not approval of Jonah's silence. The prescriptive centre lies in the questions that God asks: whether anger at mercy has any right, and whether compassion for a city is the proper response to the sight of people perishing.

The death wishes of Moses and Elijah are likewise described and not commended, though God handles each of them with great tenderness. A believer in despair can pray as they did, and find, as they did, that God meets the prayer with provision and a task rather than with rebuke. Jonah's is different because it comes out of resentment, and the chapter shows that resentment is a spiritual problem and not merely an emotional one.

What carries forward is a diagnostic. If the news of someone's repentance or forgiveness, particularly someone we regard as an enemy, produces irritation and not joy, the heart has drifted from the heart of God. Jesus tells the parable of the elder brother for exactly this reason, Luke 15:28-32, and the New Testament asks believers to love their enemies so that they may be sons of their Father in heaven, Matthew 5:44-45. The book does not say that justice is unimportant. It says that mercy rejoiced over is the mark of God's people.

debates.question: Why does the book end with an unanswered question?

views.label: A deliberate appeal to the reader
views.case: By leaving Jonah silent, the writer hands the question to us: will we share God's heart for the nations? The open ending is the book's masterstroke, refusing us a comfortable resolution.

views.label: An implied rebuke of Jonah
views.case: Jonah's silence is itself the answer; he has no reply, and the reader is meant to feel the weight of his exposed and speechless resentment.

views.label: The story we are reading is Jonah's answer
views.case: Some think the prophet must have eventually come round, since the book exists and is told with such honesty about his faults, as if Jonah himself were the source. The unfinished ending then invites the reader into the same change of heart.

debates.bearing: All three readings press the same point home: the real subject is not Jonah's fate but the reader's heart toward a God who loves those we might rather condemn. The text gives no resolution, and a reader should not invent one that lets him off.

debates.question: What is the point of the plant, the worm, and the wind?

views.label: An argument from the lesser to the greater
views.case: Jonah grieves over a plant he neither made nor grew; how much more should God, the Maker, care about a city full of living people. The lesson exposes the disproportion in Jonah's compassion, verses 10 and 11.

views.label: A mirror of Jonah's misplaced values
views.case: Jonah's joy over the plant and rage at its loss reveal a heart moved by his own comfort but unmoved by thousands of souls, holding his values up for judgment.

debates.bearing: Both readings converge: the object lesson diagnoses a heart that cares more for personal comfort than for people, and calls it to be reordered after God's own compassion.

debates.question: Who are the 120,000 who 'cannot tell their right hand from their left'?

views.label: Young children
views.case: Deuteronomy 1:39 and Isaiah 7:15-16 use the idea of not knowing good from evil for small children. On this reading the figure counts the children of Nineveh, which would imply a very large total population, and the innocence of the little ones makes the argument for mercy stronger.

views.label: The whole population as morally ignorant
views.case: Others take it as a description of a people who do not know the true God or His law, so that their evil is the evil of ignorance. This matches the way the New Testament speaks of ignorance in Acts 17:30 and Acts 3:17, and Jesus' prayer in Luke 23:34.

debates.bearing: Either way, the phrase is an appeal to pity, not an excuse. Nineveh's violence was real, but those described are people who have not been taught what God requires, and the God who has now sent them a prophet has every reason to care.

study.originalLanguages:
The first verse is stronger in Hebrew than in English. The text says the matter was 'evil to Jonah, a great evil,' and the BSB footnote shows the plain reading. The same word for evil is used for Nineveh's wickedness in Jonah 1:2 and for the disaster God spared the city in 3:10, so a single word now describes Jonah's reaction. The verb that follows means to burn, so Jonah 'burned' with anger. The same idiom is used of Cain in Genesis 4:5, and God's question to Cain, 'Why are you angry?' Genesis 4:6, is the question He now asks Jonah.

In verse 4 and again in verse 9 the question 'Have you any right to be angry?' rests on a Hebrew expression that asks whether anger is good, right or fitting. The word is built on the root for good. God does not ask whether Jonah feels angry but whether the anger is good.

Verse 2 says Jonah fled 'so quick.' The Hebrew verb is built on the root meaning to come before or to anticipate. Jonah did not merely run; he ran ahead of God's mercy, trying to get away before it could act. The prayer of verse 2 also repeats the confession of Exodus 34:6, 'compassionate and gracious,' in the order 'gracious and compassionate' as it is found in Joel 2:13 and Psalm 145:8, where Exodus 34:6 has them the other way round. The ending is different from Exodus. Jonah concludes, 'One who relents from sending disaster,' the same ending Joel gives. The expected 'faithfulness' of Exodus does not appear, and the weight falls on God's readiness to turn aside from judgment.

The plant is named in the BSB footnote as the Hebrew qiqayon, 'possibly the castor oil plant.' The word is used only in this chapter. Verse 10 says it 'sprang up in a night and perished in a night.' The Hebrew phrase is literally that it was a 'son of a night' and perished as a 'son of a night.' It is a Hebrew way of saying a thing belongs to a certain time, and it presses the transience of what Jonah has cherished.

Verse 6 joins the two names, 'the LORD God,' for the God who provides the vine, then in verses 7 and 8 the narrator calls Him simply 'God' when He sends the worm and the wind. The shift between the names is often noticed, though the narrator does not explain it, and what matters is that the same God stands behind the giving and the taking. The verb 'appointed' is used four times in the book, for the fish in Jonah 1:17 and for the vine, the worm and the wind here, which shows a single hand at work in all of them.

Verse 10 says 'You cared about the plant' with the verb meaning to have pity or to spare, which in Joel 2:17 is what the priests ask God to do: 'Spare Your people.' Jonah pities a vine, and God spares a city. God adds that Jonah neither tended the plant nor made it grow, which names the work of a gardener and a creator. The book closes by contrasting what Jonah had no hand in making with a city that God has made.

typology.type: Jonah as the resentful elder brother, Jonah 4:1-4
typology.fulfillment: Jonah's anger at a welcomed returner anticipates the elder brother who 'refused to go in' when the father welcomed the prodigal, Luke 15:28. Both are insiders who have served and resent grace to outsiders, and both are met by a patient father figure who comes out to plead. In Luke the parable stops with the question unanswered, just as Jonah does. The correspondence breaks at one point: the elder brother resents mercy to a sibling, while Jonah resents mercy to a nation.

Jonah sits outside Nineveh to watch, his heart set against it. Jesus also went outside the city, but for the opposite reason: 'Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood,' Hebrews 13:12. Jonah goes out to see judgment; Christ goes out to bear it. The comparison is a contrast, and the point is that where Jonah withdraws from the city, Christ goes outside to bring it in.

Jonah says that it is better to die than to live, because mercy has been shown to his enemies. The pattern stands against Christ's death. 'God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us,' Romans 5:8, and we were reconciled when we were enemies, Romans 5:10. Jonah would die rather than see enemies saved; Christ died so that enemies might be saved. The type is a dark mirror, and the New Testament's picture of the cross answers its rage.

typology.type: The ignorant who cannot tell right from left, Jonah 4:11
typology.fulfillment: The mercy God shows to people who 'do not know' anticipates the cross. On the cross Jesus prays, 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing,' Luke 23:34, and Peter later tells the crowd, 'I know that you acted in ignorance,' Acts 3:17. The correspondence is of attitude, mercy for the ignorant. It falls short in this: Nineveh's ignorance was addressed by a warning and a reprieve, while Christ's prayer was answered by a finished atonement.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ most sharply by contrast, because it shows a prophet who is everything Christ is not. Jonah is a man who quotes God's compassion and does not share it. Jesus is the one in whom that compassion walked among us. The prophet sits outside the city to see it fall. Jesus, approaching Jerusalem, 'saw the city, He wept over it,' Luke 19:41, and said, 'If only you had known on this day what would bring you peace.' At the end of His life He prays, 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing,' Luke 23:34, using the language of the ignorant that God uses of Nineveh's multitude in Jonah 4:11. Where Jonah wanted death for enemies, Christ gave His own death for them: 'while we were still sinners, Christ died for us,' Romans 5:8.

The chapter also leads to Christ by the problem it raises. God asks, 'should I not care about the great city of Nineveh?' and the answer is yes, but the question also hides a harder one. How can the God who 'will by no means leave the guilty unpunished,' Exodus 34:7, spare a city of violent people on the strength of a few days of sackcloth? Jonah is not troubled by the doctrine of mercy so much as by its apparent injustice. The answer the New Testament gives is that God's mercy is not a lapse of justice but a purchase at the cross. 'God presented Him as the atoning sacrifice... to demonstrate His righteousness,' Romans 3:25. Mercy to Nineveh was made safe by a death Nineveh did not know about.

Jesus also tells the parables that grow from this chapter. The elder brother who stays outside the feast in Luke 15:28-32 and the workers who grumble that the last were paid as the first in Matthew 20:1-15 are the same figure as Jonah under his shelter. In each, the point is that the owner's generosity is not unfairness. 'Are you envious because I am generous?' Matthew 20:15. Christ is the host who comes out to plead with the angry guest, and He does so at the cost of His own life.

There is also a way in which Jesus is the better Jonah. Jonah's account ends with his reluctance. Jesus, who calls Himself greater than Jonah, Matthew 12:41, did not flee the commission. He set His face toward Jerusalem, endured the cross, 'scorning its shame,' Hebrews 12:2, and has now sent His church to the nations to do what Jonah would not. Paul draws the large conclusion, 'God has consigned everyone to disobedience so that He may have mercy on everyone,' Romans 11:32.

The chapter should not be turned into an allegory of every detail. The vine is not Christ, and the worm is not Satan. The texts above rest on the way the New Testament reads mercy, enemies and the ignorant, and on Jesus' own use of Jonah. What the chapter supplies is the disease, a heart that resents grace, and what Christ supplies is both the diagnosis and the cure.
study.god:
The most striking thing in this chapter is that God does not defend Himself by force. Jonah has just told Him to His face that mercy is an evil and that he would rather die. God's answer is a question, 'Have you any right to be angry?' verse 4. He appoints a plant, then a worm, then a wind, and then asks again. The almighty God argues patiently with a sulking prophet. His authority is total, since vine, worm and wind each come at His appointment, but He uses it to teach and not to crush. The same hand that sent the fish and the storm in chapter 1 now sends shade and then heat. That is God's way with a servant He means to bring home.

The chapter shows God as the one who owns and cares for what He has made. Jonah did not plant the vine or make it grow. Nineveh's people, and even its cattle, belong to Him. Psalm 36:6 says 'You preserve man and beast,' and Psalm 145:9 says 'His compassion rests on all He has made.' When God says 'should I not care about the great city,' He is speaking as Creator, and His compassion is not sentimental but grounded in ownership and care. The mention of cattle in the last verse shows how far this care extends. God's compassion also reaches those who 'cannot tell their right hand from their left,' meaning those who are ignorant of Him, which echoes Acts 17:30, where God overlooked the ignorance of earlier times and now commands all to repent.

The chapter shows God's character stated by Jonah himself: gracious, compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion, and ready to relent from sending disaster. These are not four independent attributes but one description of a God who delights in mercy, as Micah 7:18 will say, 'He delights in loving devotion.' The book insists that this is not the weakness of a God who ignores sin. Chapter 1 shows Him sending a storm on a disobedient prophet, and chapter 3 shows a real threat against a violent city. The mercy of God is the mercy of a Judge who warns before He strikes and who is moved by repentance.

He is also free. 'I will have mercy on whom I have mercy,' Romans 9:15. Jonah cannot compel God to destroy, and Nineveh could not compel Him to spare. Mercy is given, not owed, and this is exactly what Jonah cannot bear. A God who is free to forgive an enemy is also free to forgive Jonah, a truth the prophet needs more than he realises.

For worship, the chapter calls us to rejoice in the right place. We are to praise God for the same attributes in His treatment of our enemies that we praise in His treatment of ourselves. We are also invited to stand under His questions with an open heart. The book shows a God who would rather be answered than obeyed grudgingly, and who is willing to wait for the answer.

crossReferences.note: The words Jonah throws back at God are the words God first spoke to Moses about Himself. In Exodus they come as a revelation of His glory; in Jonah they come as a grievance. The comparison shows that the content of the creed was never in dispute, only whether Jonah would share the joy of it.

Joel uses almost the same creed to summon Judah to return, and adds, 'Who knows? He may turn and relent.' The creed works as a ground of hope for the repentant. Jonah turns the same creed into a reason for fury, which shows how the same truth lands on a humble heart and a hard one.

Cain was very angry, and God asked him, 'Why are you angry?' and warned him that sin crouches at the door. The question God puts to Jonah is the question put to the first angry man in Scripture. Both speak with patience, and both are left with a choice about how to master the anger.

Elijah, after a great victory, runs from Jezebel and prays under a broom tree, 'Take my life.' God feeds him and sends him on. The similarity with Jonah's prayer shows that despair among prophets was a known pattern, and the difference shows that Jonah's cause is resentment and not exhaustion.

The little ones 'who on that day did not know good from evil' are allowed into the land. The same idea sits behind the 120,000 who cannot tell right from left in Jonah 4:11. It supports reading the phrase as an appeal to pity for people without the moral understanding to know what they were doing.

The psalm repeats the confession Jonah quotes and goes on to say, 'The LORD is good to all; His compassion rests on all He has made.' This is the doctrine behind God's closing question. His compassion does not stop at Israel's border or at the edge of the human race, because it covers all He made.

The workers who came last are paid the same as those who came first, and the early workers grumble. The owner replies, 'Are you envious because I am generous?' Jesus tells it to the same kind of audience as Jonah's, and the answer to Jonah's anger is the same: the generosity is God's to give.

The elder brother is angry at his brother's welcome and refuses to go in, and the father comes out to plead with him. Like Jonah, he has been faithful on the outside and resentful within. Luke leaves the story unfinished, just as Jonah does, so that the hearer must decide whether to join the feast.

Jesus weeps over Jerusalem as He draws near to it, grieved for a city that will not know the things that make for its peace. The contrast with Jonah, sitting outside Nineveh waiting for its fall, could hardly be sharper. Here is the heart of God in a human face.

Paul sums up the history of mercy: Gentiles have received mercy through Israel's disobedience, and Israel will receive mercy through the mercy shown to the Gentiles. God has shut everyone up in disobedience so that He may have mercy on everyone. It is the theology behind God's question to Jonah.

The next prophet in the Twelve asks, 'Who is a God like You, who pardons iniquity,' and says that God 'delights in loving devotion.' Micah makes Jonah's creed into praise. It is the response Jonah ought to have given, and the book of Micah gives it on behalf of the people.

study.oneStory:
The story of Scripture is the story of God's creation, its fall into rebellion, and His determination to rescue it. Jonah 4 sits at the point where that rescue is tested against the heart of the rescued. God had made humanity and called a people through Abraham so that the families of the earth would be blessed, Genesis 12:3. Israel's calling was a vocation to the nations, as Isaiah says, and Jonah is the prophet who is asked to carry it out. Chapter 4 reveals that the greatest obstacle to the mission is not the nations' hardness but the messenger's.

That is not a new problem in the Bible. Cain is angry before God and murders his brother, Genesis 4:5-8. The brothers of Joseph resent a favoured sibling. Israel at Sinai makes a calf and is spared because of God's character, Exodus 34:6. Jonah's problem is the human problem: the sinner who has received grace believes that grace belongs to him and his kind. The book is a mirror held up to everyone who has been rescued.

The question God asks at the end sets up the New Testament. A greater prophet than Jonah comes who does not wait outside the city for it to fall but weeps over it, Luke 19:41, goes outside the gate to die for it, Hebrews 13:12, and prays for His killers' forgiveness, Luke 23:34. In Him the mercy of God stops being an unexplained mystery and becomes an accomplished act. Paul says that Gentiles who were 'far away' have now been 'brought near through the blood of Christ,' Ephesians 2:13, and that God has bound everyone in disobedience so that He may have mercy on everyone, Romans 11:32. The commission that Jonah resisted is given to the church, and Peter learns on a rooftop that God 'does not show favoritism,' Acts 10:34.

The new creation completes what the book begins. The people God gathers are a multitude no one could count, from every nation, tribe, people and tongue, Revelation 7:9. Among them will be those who were once enemies and have become family. Whether Jonah is among them, the book does not say. His silence is left open so that each reader may answer for himself, and the hope of the whole Bible is that the answer will be what the Lord wanted from His prophet: a heart that rejoices when a lost city is found.

sermon.title: Amazing Grace
sermon.why: From Begg's expository series A Study in Jonah, this message treats the close of the book, Jonah 4:5-11, the plant, the worm, and God's final question, showing the breadth of God's grace against the prophet's resentment. A clear, orthodox handling of this movement's climax.

quiz.q: Why was Jonah so angry after Nineveh was spared?

options.text: He resented God showing mercy to his enemies; it is the reason he fled in the first place.
options.note: Jonah 4:2 has him admit he fled because he knew God was gracious and would relent.

options.text: He was embarrassed that his prophecy of destruction did not come true.
options.note: Wounded pride may play a part, but the text names resentment of mercy as the root.

options.text: He was exhausted from the long journey to Nineveh.
options.note: His anger is moral and spiritual, not mere tiredness.

options.text: He was angry that God had not given him a reward.
options.note: The issue is grace to enemies, not any missing reward.

quiz.q: What was the point of the plant, the worm, and the wind?

options.text: To show that if Jonah pitied a mere plant, how much more should God pity a city of people.
options.note: Jonah 4:10-11 argues from the lesser to the greater to expose his misplaced compassion.

options.text: To punish Jonah for his disobedience.
options.note: It is teaching more than punishment; God is reasoning with him, not merely disciplining him.

options.text: To give Jonah comfort in the heat.
options.note: The plant gave brief comfort, but its removal was the lesson, not the comfort itself.

options.text: To show that God controls the weather.
options.note: God's sovereignty is assumed, but the point is compassion for people.

quiz.q: How does the book of Jonah end?

options.text: With God's unanswered question about caring for Nineveh, left hanging for the reader.
options.note: The open ending presses the question of compassion onto us, Jonah 4:11.

options.text: With Jonah repenting and rejoicing over the city.
options.note: We might hope for this, but the text leaves Jonah silent and the question open.

options.text: With Nineveh being destroyed after all.
options.note: Nineveh was spared; the tension is over Jonah's heart, not the city's ruin.

options.text: With God punishing Jonah for his anger.
options.note: God reasons with Jonah in patience rather than punishing him.

quiz.q: How does Jonah's attitude contrast with Jesus?

options.text: Jonah resented mercy to enemies and wanted them dead; Jesus loved His enemies and died praying for their forgiveness.
options.note: Jonah is the foil that magnifies the compassion of Christ, Luke 23:34.

options.text: Both struggled equally to love their enemies.
options.note: Jesus did not struggle to love enemies; He gave His life for them, unlike Jonah.

options.text: Jonah is a perfect model of Christlike mercy.
options.note: Jonah models the opposite of Christ's mercy here.

options.text: There is no meaningful contrast between them.
options.note: The contrast is stark and deliberate, throwing Christ's mercy into relief.

quiz.q: What does God's closing question reveal about His heart?

options.text: He genuinely cares about people who do not yet know Him, and longs to spare rather than destroy.
options.note: God's final word is compassion for a whole city, the heart behind 2 Peter 3:9.

options.text: He cares mainly about being proved right.
options.note: God's concern is for the people themselves, not for winning an argument.

options.text: He is indifferent to what happens to Nineveh.
options.note: The whole point is that He is far from indifferent; He cares deeply.

options.text: He values plants over people.
options.note: The argument runs the opposite way: people matter far more than a plant.

questions: Jonah admitted he ran because God was too merciful for his liking. Is there any way you resent grace being shown to people you feel do not deserve it?
Jonah cared more about a plant, and his own comfort, than about a city full of people. Where have your own comforts crowded out compassion for those who are lost?
God reasoned patiently with an angry, sulking prophet instead of striking him down. How does His patience with Jonah encourage you in your own failures and resentments?
The book ends with God's question hanging in the air, and no reply from Jonah. If God asked you that question about the people you would rather avoid, how would you answer?
Jesus is the true and better Jonah, who wept over the city and died for His enemies. How does His compassion move you to pray for and reach the very people you once feared or despised?

translationNotes.note: Greatly displeased renders a Hebrew phrase meaning it was exceedingly evil to Jonah, using the same word, ra'ah, applied earlier to Nineveh's wickedness and the threatened disaster.
Jonah quotes the ancient confession of God's character from Exodus 34:6, gracious, compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion, chesed.
The plant is the Hebrew qiqayon, possibly the castor oil plant, as the BSB footnote notes; the same plant is meant in verses 7, 9, and 10.
Who cannot tell their right hand from their left likely pictures the vast number of people, perhaps stressing the young or the spiritually ignorant, all of them objects of God's care.
